newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Church of Scientology ex-leader sentenced. [CORRECTED]
newsitem.headline: French Church of Scientology ex-leader sentenced. [CORRECTED]

text.p: A court on Friday sentenced the former head of the Church of Scientology in Lyon, central France (corrects to clarify that Mazier was former head of church in Lyon, not all France) to 18 months jail for manslaughter and fraud in a case stemming from a follower's suicide.

After an eight-day trial in October, the court jailed Jean-Jacques Mazier and handed down suspended sentences on 14 other defendants tied to the organisation on charges ranging from embezzlement to fraud, and acquitted eight others.
Scientology spokesman Marc Bromberg said the church would appeal against the sentences, which he described as scandalous, politically-motivated and a breach of freedom of religion.

At the trial in Lyon, central France, prosecutors sought to portray the organisation as an enterprise masquerading as a religion, whose chief function was to extort cash from the gullible using abusive high-pressure techniques.
Defence lawyers countered that the organisation was a legitimate religion and argued that their clients were the innocent victims of a campaign by the centre-right government to crack down on cults.
State prosecutor Thierry Ricard had asked the court to sentence 21 of the 23 defendants in the dock to suspended jail terms and fines of up to 500,000 francs ($100,000).
He had recommended a three-year suspended sentence for Mazier, who was accused of manslaughter and fraud in the 1988 suicide of scientology follower Patrice Vic.
The prosecution said Mazier went to the home of Vic, a 30-year-old industrial designer, where both men put pressure on Vic's wife to lend him money to attend a scientology course.
Unable to raise the money, Vic threw himself off his high-rise apartment block. The defence blamed the suicide on long-term depression and alcohol abuse.

The trial was prompted by Vic's widow Nelly, who accused the organisation of driving him to debt and despair. After delays, it was finally brought to trial after the government announced it was stepping up its campaign against cults in France.
Defence lawyer Benoit Ducos Ader argued that all 23 defendants were innocent and insisted that the court lacked jurisdiction in any case.
But Ricard told the court: "The Church of Scientology is an international sect whose goals are commercial and dangerous methods disruptive to public order."
The trial revolved around whether the Church of Scientology, founded in 1954 by the late American science-fiction novelist L. Ron Hubbard, was a sect or a religion.
As a religion, it could legally ask members to give it funds.

The church claims more than eight million adherents worldwide, including 40,000 in France. One of its teachings is that the problems of the human race are linked to disembodied souls brought to the planet millions of years ago.
Members include Hollywood film stars Tom Cruise, his Australian-born wife Nicole Kidman, John Travolta, Kirstie Alley and Lisa Marie Presley, daughter of the legendary rock star.
